raw_response:
I am 68 years old and I have worked this land in Quzhou County for 50 years. My household is just my wife and me now — our son works in a factory over in Handan, so he sends some money home but he does not farm. I manage 6 mu of stevia, which I switched to from grain crops several years ago because the leaf buyers pay cash and the income is steadier than gambling on corn prices.

Last season I got about 140 kg of dry leaves per mu, but my soil is getting tired. I took a sample to the county agricultural station last winter, and the test showed available phosphorus down to 12 mg/kg and nitrogen depleted after years of heavy leaf crops. Potassium was still at medium level. This year I am adjusting my inputs based on that report, not just copying what I did before.

For basal fertilizer, I put down one 50-kg bag of compound fertilizer per mu — 15-15-15 — which gives me 7.5 kg each of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium. Then I add 20 kg of superphosphate per mu to push phosphorus up to about 10 kg total, because the soil test flagged that deficiency. Stevia is a leaf crop and it needs nitrogen to build canopy, so I split-apply urea in three passes: 10 kg per mu at transplanting in late April, another 10 kg per mu right after the first cutting in early July when the regrowth starts, and 8 kg per mu in mid-August for the second flush. Counting the nitrogen from the compound bag, that brings me to about 16 kg of nitrogen per mu for the whole season. I do not add extra potassium — the 7.5 kg from the basal dressing is enough, and muriate of potash is expensive this year at the dealer.

Irrigation comes from my well. I will run water 8 times: immediately after transplanting, then every 10 to 14 days through May and June when the leaf expansion is fastest. In July and August I watch the sky — if we get a solid rain I skip a round, but I do not let the field stress for water during the cutting periods. A dry spell during leaf fill would drop my yield by 20 kg per mu easy, and that costs far more than the electricity for pumping.

For pests, I spray 3 times. First is preventive against aphids in late May when the weather turns warm. Second is in early July after the first harvest — fresh-cut stevia attracts insects. Third is in mid-September before the final cutting, for leaf spot and late caterpillars. I buy generic imidacloprid and mancozeb from the village input shop. Three well-timed sprays are enough; spraying every week just wastes money.

Tillage is rotary — I hire my neighbor Lao Zhang to run his machine through in early April. Costs me 200 yuan for the 6 mu. Deep ploughing is unnecessary for stevia roots, and at 68 I am not interested in extra labor. I plant an improved variety that the county extension introduced three years ago. It out-yields the old traditional type by a clear margin, and the glycoside content meets the buyer's standard.

My cash cost runs about 1,100 yuan per mu. If I hit 150 kg per mu and the dried leaf price stays at 13 yuan per kg, I clear roughly 850 yuan per mu after paying for inputs and hired machine work. I thought about cutting back on fertilizer to save money because my wife's medicine costs have gone up, but doing the math, saving 80 yuan per mu on urea is foolish if it risks losing 15 kg of yield per mu. A bad harvest is a disaster I cannot afford; an extra bag of fertilizer is just a cost I absorb.
